selected.title: What can a hearth and post mark reveal about people 13,800 years ago?
selected.summary: Researchers report a 13,800-year-old Alaska camp with a hearth, a post stain, tools, needles and other remains. They describe the structure as a potential early dwelling, not a definitive house.
selected.why_it_matters: Evidence of a dwelling can reshape understanding of how early communities organized life and adapted to the far north after reaching the Americas.
selected.challenge_question: What is the strongest claim researchers make about the Alaska structure?
selected.answer_explanation: The study describes the features as the earliest potential evidence of a habitation structure in North America. The remains include a hearth and a dirt stain interpreted as a former wooden post; the interpretation remains cautious.
selected.butterfly_question: How would evidence of settled camps change the story of migration and survival in the Americas?

selected.title: Could one new undersea cable move 125 terabytes every second?
selected.summary: Meta announced Petal, a planned 7,000-kilometer cable linking the U.S. and France. The company says it could carry up to one petabit per second when it comes online in 2029.
selected.why_it_matters: More transatlantic capacity could change where data-intensive services run and how quickly they reach users, while increasing reliance on ocean-floor infrastructure.
selected.challenge_question: What is the planned Petal cable’s maximum stated capacity?
selected.answer_explanation: Meta’s stated maximum is one petabit per second, equivalent to one million gigabits per second. The cable is planned to connect the United States and France and is expected online in 2029.
selected.butterfly_question: If data capacity becomes abundant, what becomes the next constraint: electricity, computing, or access?

selected.title: What becomes scarce when internet bandwidth surges?
selected.summary: A proposed transatlantic undersea cable is designed to carry up to one petabit per second. Its launch is planned for 2029, so the capacity remains a future target rather than a live service.
selected.why_it_matters: A sharp increase in backbone capacity may shift bottlenecks toward data centers, power supply and network access instead of long-distance transmission alone.
selected.challenge_question: When is Petal expected to come online, according to current reports?
selected.answer_explanation: The report gives 2029 as the expected online date. Because the cable is still planned, both the schedule and the stated capacity should be treated as company targets, not completed infrastructure.
selected.butterfly_question: If the cable is no longer the bottleneck, which infrastructure will struggle next to keep data moving?

selected.title: What new species might be hiding in museum drawers?
selected.summary: A fossil collected about a century ago was identified as Invictibellatrix amberina, a previously unknown megaraptoran dinosaur. Researchers say it is the first megaraptoran identified in Europe.
selected.why_it_matters: Re-examining old collections can reveal species and evolutionary histories without finding new excavation sites, changing what museums can teach about ancient ecosystems.
selected.challenge_question: Where was the newly identified dinosaur fossil found before its study?
selected.answer_explanation: The fossil had been in a museum collection for roughly a century before researchers recognized it as a distinct megaraptoran species. The report highlights the scientific value of reexamining historical collections.
selected.butterfly_question: If old collections contain undiscovered species, how should museums prioritize re-studying what they already hold?

selected.title: When does a floating seaweed habitat become a coastal burden?
selected.summary: A recent science broadcast highlights a surge of floating sargassum affecting Atlantic coastlines. Offshore, the algae also provides habitat and food for marine species, making the bloom’s impacts complex.
selected.why_it_matters: The same drifting algae can support ocean ecosystems offshore and create costly coastal problems when it washes ashore, linking marine ecology, tourism and community response.
selected.challenge_question: What makes large sargassum blooms ecologically complicated?
selected.answer_explanation: NOAA describes floating sargassum as habitat and food for marine species, while also noting that large accumulations washing ashore can harm communities. That contrast is the central ecological trade-off.
selected.butterfly_question: Can coastal communities remove stranded seaweed without damaging the marine life that depends on it offshore?
